item.title: eto — Wednesday, July 29, 2026
item.description: The Wednesday, July 29, 2026 edition: 8 stories, each one event told through outlets that disagree.
item.content:encoded:
Trump meets with Zelenskyy, Netanyahu at Lindsey Graham funeral services.

President Donald Trump met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday as part of the funeral services for late Senator Lindsey Graham. The meeting reflects their respect for Graham and recognition of his loss in their relationships with Trump and Washington. Trump will meet with each world leader separately before the funeral.

Graham was a tenacious advocate for Israel and Ukraine, and he will leave a void, as few political leaders can match his level of support, NPR's Franco Ordoñez tells Up First. Zelenskyy and Netanyahu will now need to make the case themselves to Trump that Graham once made for them.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts from different outlets conflict on several points. Al Jazeera reports that Netanyahu is primarily in the US to attend the funeral ceremony of Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, who died on July 11 (Account 2). However, The Hill states that Netanyahu's meeting with Trump will be his first in Washington since the breakout of the Iran war in February (Account 5).

Additionally, UPI reports that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky were among those who eulogized Senator Lindsey Graham at the funeral service (Account 6). However, The Hill states that both leaders plan to meet with Trump at the White House while they're in the US (Account 5).

Sources NPR · Al Jazeera · Newsweek · BBC · The Hill · UPI

Former US government science adviser Anthony Fauci's private diary entries reveal growing disillusionment with Donald Trump during Covid-19 pandemic.

The diary entries of former top US government science adviser Anthony Fauci have been released by Republican senator Rand Paul. The entries show Fauci's growing disillusionment with Donald Trump, whom he branded "rambling", "crazy", "desperate", "bumbling", "incompetent", "an idiot", "a true embarrassment", "totally nuts" and "truly an obnoxious adolescent". Fauci noted in his journal challenging interactions with the publicity-fixated Trump from the earliest days of the crisis six years ago. On 27 February 2020, amid the first stirrings of public alarm, he wrote of a surprise late-night call, in which the US president "wanted to chat about the coronavirus situation in general". Fauci encouraged Trump not to underplay the seriousness of the situation, but the next day, he again underplayed it. By 14 March, Fauci was bemoaning Trump's fixation on "the fluff of ratings and publicity".

Where the accounts differ

The accounts conflict over the number of diary entries released by Rand Paul (1,000 pages in The Hill vs. over 1,100 pages in NPR). The Guardian reports that Fauci branded Trump "an idiot" and "a true embarrassment", while FOX News focuses on Fauci's private diary entries revealing his fixation on personal fame during the pandemic. New York Post reports that Fauci privately ruled out a wet market in Wuhan as the source of the pandemic, contradicting his public statements. The Federalist lists 10 questions for Congress to ask Fauci about his Covid corruption and coverup.

Sources The Guardian · The Hill · FOX News · New York Post · The Federalist · NPR

US Senate confirms Jay Clayton as Director of National Intelligence

The US Senate has confirmed Jay Clayton as the next Director of National Intelligence (DNI) in a 51-47 vote, replacing acting DNI Bill Pulte. Clayton, who was serving as the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York, will oversee the country's 18 intelligence agencies. The confirmation comes after President Donald Trump's original choice, Tulsi Gabbard, resigned last month and was temporarily replaced by Pulte.

Clayton has a background in law and finance, having previously served as chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission. He was nominated to replace Pulte, who faced criticism for his lack of national security experience. Clayton's confirmation is seen as a victory for Trump, who had been pushing for his appointment despite opposition from Democrats.

The confirmation vote comes amid a heightened threat environment, with some lawmakers expressing concerns about the impact on national security. Senate Majority Leader John Thune praised Clayton's qualifications, saying he has "significant national security experience" and will be a "proven leader in this role."

Where the accounts differ

  • The BBC reports that Pulte was Trump's original choice for DNI, while Washington Examiner states that Gabbard was the original nominee. (BBC, Washington Examiner)
  • The New York Post notes that Clayton's confirmation hearing was delayed due to Trump's request, citing his increased push for the SAVE America Act. This is not mentioned in other accounts. (New York Post)
  • FOX News reports that Senate Democrats demanded a new, experienced person to lead the nation's spy agencies, but when given the chance, they rejected President Donald Trump's latest pick. Washington Examiner states that Democrats welcomed Clayton as a more conventional nominee than Pulte. (FOX News, Washington Examiner)

Sources BBC · Washington Examiner · New York Post · FOX News · Just The News

A 6.8-magnitude earthquake strikes Kumamoto, Japan, causing widespread damage and at least 13 deaths.

A powerful earthquake struck Kumamoto, Japan on Tuesday, leaving a trail of destruction and at least 13 dead. The quake, which measured 6.8 magnitude according to the US Geological Survey, caused widespread damage and power outages in the region. Rescue efforts are underway, with emergency services working to reach trapped individuals.

The earthquake also triggered a tsunami advisory, although it was later lifted within two hours. Aeon Mall Kumamoto, a shopping center that had recently reopened after years of reconstruction following a 2016 earthquake, suffered significant damage and an explosion occurred shortly after the quake. At least 50 people were injured in the blast, with many more feared trapped inside.

Rescue operations are ongoing, with hundreds of first responders from neighboring prefectures arriving on Tuesday evening to assist. The Japanese military has mobilized 3,600 personnel for disaster relief operations, and 20 aircraft have been sent to assess damage from the air.

Where the accounts differ

  • Straight Arrow News reports that a highway bridge buckled due to the earthquake, while UPI does not mention this detail.
  • Al Jazeera states that an explosion ripped through Aeon Mall Kumamoto shortly after the quake, while FOX News reports that witnesses smelled gas before the explosion.
  • The Guardian notes that relatively few buildings collapsed in the region, despite the intensity of the quake, due to Japan's strict construction standards and earthquake resistance requirements. This detail is not mentioned by other outlets.

Sources Straight Arrow News · UPI · Al Jazeera · Newsweek · The Guardian · FOX News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Former President Joe Biden's ghostwriter tapes released after two-year court battle

The Oversight Project, a conservative watchdog group, has released nearly 70 hours of audio recordings made by former President Joe Biden with his ghostwriter Mark Zwonitzer in 2016 and 2017. The recordings were cited in former special counsel Robert Hur's 2024 report on Biden's handling of classified documents. According to the report, Biden kept volumes of notes at his home that included classified information.

The tapes reveal Biden discussing potentially sensitive meetings, including "a big meeting with the CIA and everyone," "a big meeting down in the Situation Room," and "a long meeting where DOD brief ... POTUS." In one recording, Biden tells Zwonitzer that he has extensive notes over a period of time, which were not known to the White House. He also says, "I just found all the classified stuff downstairs."

Biden's conversations with Zwonitzer show him struggling to remember certain details or dates regarding events and topics in the transcripts and recordings. At one point, Biden seems to lose his train of thought: "Alright — what was I going to ask you? Something else… Uh… um. Oh gosh. I can't think of anything else."

Where the accounts differ

The accounts from The Guardian and CBS News report that the tapes were released after a two-year court battle by the Oversight Project, while The Daily Wire reports that Biden's lawyers fought to keep the tapes private. The New York Post states that the tapes were previously scrutinized by former special counsel Robert Hur as part of his 2023-2024 investigation into Joe Biden's retention of classified documents.

The Washington Examiner and CBS News report that Biden told Zwonitzer that some material may be classified, while The Guardian reports that Biden appears to discuss sensitive information on tape with his ghostwriter. The Daily Wire states that the tapes reveal Biden's inability to remember basic names and dates.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Guardian · CBS News · The Daily Wire · FOX News · New York Post

No source labeled center covered this story.

Canadian tourism numbers decline in US amid trade tensions and tariffs.

The Canadian government released a report detailing declining tourism numbers to the US, with Canadians making 29.1 million trips to the US in 2025, down from 39 million the year before. The report blames President Donald Trump's administration for the decline, citing his recent tariffs and other tensions between the countries as contributing factors.

However, other factors may also be at play. In years prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, there were fewer Canadian trips to the US than in 2025, with just 25 million trips in 2019. The lifting of COVID-19 restrictions in late 2022 may have contributed to higher numbers in 2023 and 2024.

The decline in numbers could also be due to costs associated with Trump's tariffs, which may be deterring Canadian travelers who are not feeling the same effects.

Where the accounts differ

Straight Arrow News reports that Canadians made 29.1 million trips to the US in 2025, while The Guardian states that Canadians spent $3.3bn less on travel to the US in 2025 than in the previous year. CBS News also reports a decline of roughly 25% in visits by Canadians to the US in 2025.

The Free Press provides context on the trade tensions and tariffs between Canada and the US, citing the White House's use of Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 as a provision aimed directly at Canada. Straight Arrow News does not mention this specific provision.

Straight Arrow News notes that Canadian tourism has seen a steady month-to-month increase so far in 2026, while The Guardian reports that return trips to Canada from the US are at similar levels seen at the end of 2025.

Sources Straight Arrow News · The Free Press · The Guardian · CBS News

No source labeled right covered this story.

Trump administration asks Supreme Court to allow enforcement of mail-in voting executive order.

The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to lift a lower court's block on an executive order aimed at tightening rules on mail-in voting ahead of the midterm elections in November. The executive order, issued in March, directs federal agencies to create state-by-state lists of eligible mail voters and would prevent the U.S. Postal Service from delivering ballots to people not included on those lists.

The administration argues that the lower court's injunction was premature because the agencies have not yet implemented any policy changes. Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in a petition to the Supreme Court that "the Order merely sets forth general policy guidance, leaving substantial discretion to agencies about how to implement the Order while admonishing them that they may do so only consistent with applicable law."

The lower court's block on the executive order was upheld by an appeals court, which agreed that the president lacks the authority to unilaterally change how federal elections are administered. The states challenging the order argue that the Constitution gives states and Congress, not the president, the authority to set election rules.

Where the accounts differ

  • The accounts from different outlets conflict on several points.
  • UPI reports that Trump has claimed, without evidence, that there are widespread issues with voter fraud benefiting Democrats in the 2020 presidential election. This claim is not made by any other outlet.
  • The Washington Examiner and Straight Arrow News report that Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued that the injunction was premature because agencies had not yet implemented policy changes. UPI reports this argument, but does not attribute it to Sauer.
  • The Guardian reports that Trump's proposed changes are "ripe for abuse" and could cause chaos, a characterization made by Democratic officials in 23 states and the District of Columbia, as reported by all outlets.

Sources The Federalist · UPI · Straight Arrow News · Washington Examiner · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: White Phosphorous Leak At US Military Base Sparks Evacuation

White phosphorus leak reported at US military base in South Korea

South Korean authorities ordered civilians to evacuate after a suspected white phosphorus leak at the Osan Air Base near Seoul. The alert was lifted several hours later following decontamination work, according to text messages sent out by the city of Pyeongtaek. The U.S. 51st Fighter Wing said it established a cordon around the base "out of an abundance of caution" after experts identified white phosphorus crystallization inside a munitions crate.

The incident occurred at Osan Air Base, which is home to the U.S. Air Force's 51st Fighter Wing. The base commander, Col. Ryan Ley, said that the safety of service members and their families was the top priority. White phosphorus is a chemical substance used in incendiary munitions and smoke shells.

The cordon around the base was lifted after emergency response personnel mitigated the situation, allowing normal operations to resume. There were "no injuries resulting from this situation and no risk to personnel on or off installation," according to the U.S. 51st Fighter Wing.

Where the accounts differ

Associated Press reports that a 300-meter cordon was established around the base, while Newsweek states it was a 1,000-foot cordon. Associated Press does not mention the use of white phosphorus in incendiary munitions or smoke shells, but instead describes it as "a controversial chemical substance." Newsweek provides more context about the use of white phosphorus and its implications.

Sources Associated Press · Newsweek

No source labeled lean-right or left or right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

US and Iran appear to pause hostilities as Trump gives "diplomacy a chance"

The United States and Iran seem to have paused their military actions against each other, with President Trump indicating that he is giving diplomacy a chance. This comes after nearly two weeks of intense fighting between the two countries, which has resulted in significant losses on both sides.

According to reports, the US has not launched any strikes against Iranian targets since Thursday, and Iran has also refrained from attacking US interests. The pause in hostilities has been attributed to efforts by Pakistani and Qatari mediators to bring the two sides back to the negotiating table.

The US has reportedly made significant progress in its talks with Oman, which is working on a mechanism to manage vessels' passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's foreign ministry spokesman confirmed that talks with Oman were continuing, focused on creating necessary arrangements regarding the strait.

Trump has stated that he wants to give diplomacy a chance and that "friendly talks are underway" with Iran. However, he also warned that the US could still "cripple Iran with full force" if negotiations fail.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News reports that Trump said the US has plenty of ammunition, contradicting earlier reports of stockpile concerns. The Hill notes that Netanyahu's meeting with Trump will be his first in Washington since the breakout of the Iran war in February. Straight Arrow News highlights the Pentagon's change in how it counts casualties, separating public totals from the Iran war across two parts of its database.

Sources CBS News · The Hill · Straight Arrow News

Sen. Rand Paul releases over 1,000 pages of Dr. Anthony Fauci's diary entries from COVID-19 pandemic.

Dr. Anthony Fauci's diary entries, released by Sen. Rand Paul (R-KY), provide a glimpse into the former Chief Medical Advisor to the President's thoughts and interactions during the COVID-19 pandemic. The entries span from December 2019 to December 2022 and cover various topics, including Fauci's relationship with President Trump, his media appearances, and his views on the origins of the virus.

Fauci's diary entries reveal a complex and often tumultuous relationship with President Trump. In one entry, Fauci wrote that Trump "wanted to chat about the coronavirus situation in general" during a surprise late-night call on February 27, 2020. However, Fauci noted that Trump underplayed the seriousness of the situation the next day.

Fauci also expressed frustration with Trump's fixation on media attention and his desire for Fauci to appear on TV more frequently. In one entry, Fauci wrote that he told Trump that he was being blocked from TV appearances because he wanted to avoid being pitted against the President or Vice President.

The diary entries also show Fauci's growing disillusionment with Trump as the pandemic progressed. By March 2021, Fauci had written that Trump was "truly an obnoxious adolescent."

Where the accounts differ

  • The Daily Wire and Just The News report on Fauci's diary entries in more detail than other outlets, including his interactions with President Trump.
  • NPR focuses on the disagreement between Sen. Rand Paul and Dr. Anthony Fauci over the origins of the COVID-19 virus, while CBS News and The Hill provide a broader overview of the diary entries.
  • The Guardian highlights Fauci's criticism of Trump's handling of the pandemic, including his description of Trump as "rambling," "crazy," and "incompetent."
  • Just The News reports that Fauci considered some of the media attention during the pandemic to be "flattering," while The Hill notes that Fauci was aware of the negative impacts of the attention on him and his family.

Sources The Daily Wire · NPR · CBS News · The Guardian · Just The News · The Hill

Three people killed and four others wounded in shooting at Seattle food festival.

A shooting occurred on Sunday evening during the Bite of Seattle food festival, an annual event that attracts 350,000 people over three days. According to authorities, two suspects were involved in a shootout, with one suspect surrendering at the scene and the other remaining at large. Three people were killed, including two men aged 19 and 44, and a 56-year-old woman. Four others were wounded, including a toddler who is currently in stable condition.

The shooting happened around 6:00 p.m. local time, with police arriving on the scene shortly after. One suspect was taken into custody "within seconds," according to Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson. The investigation is ongoing, and authorities are reviewing security footage and interviewing witnesses.

Where the accounts differ

  • The Daily Wire reports that a 15-year-old and a 19-year-old were identified as suspects, while other outlets only mention two suspects.
  • FOX News reports that a third suspect may have been involved in the shooting, citing court documents. However, this is not mentioned by other outlets.
  • The Guardian mentions that the Gun Violence Archive has reported over 270 mass shootings in the US so far this year, but this information is not present in other accounts.
  • Al Jazeera and BBC report that Assistant Seattle Police Chief Tyrone Davis stated there was no ongoing threat to the public, while The Daily Wire does not mention this statement.

Sources The Daily Wire · The Guardian · Al Jazeera · BBC · FOX News · UPI

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Mitch McConnell's office shares new photo and update on senator's recovery from June fall.

Mitch McConnell, the 84-year-old Republican senator from Kentucky, has been recovering at a rehabilitation facility after a medical episode at his Washington, D.C., home last month. His office released a statement and a new photo of him with his wife, Elaine Chao, on Monday, saying he is "still working hard" to resume his full schedule in the Senate and in Kentucky. McConnell has been absent from the Senate since June 14, when he was hospitalized after taking a fall.

McConnell's office confirmed that he will miss an annual political picnic in his home state while he recovers. In a statement, McConnell said he is "looking forward to getting back to the Senate and to Kentucky soon." His attending physician also confirmed that he is not yet medically cleared to leave the rehab facility and return to the office.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts from The Hill and Newsweek report that Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) said a person who recently visited McConnell described him as "clear-minded." However, this claim is not mentioned in any other outlet.

The Daily Wire reports that McConnell's office releases a new photo plus a statement saying he is undergoing "intense physical therapy" and not ready to get back to work in person. This detail is also present in Newsweek but absent from The Hill.

Just The News does not mention the claim about McConnell being described as "clear-minded."

The Washington Examiner reports that Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) recently called on McConnell to resign if he cannot be more publicly transparent about his health, which is not mentioned in any other outlet.

Sources The Hill · New York Post · The Daily Wire · Newsweek · Just The News · Washington Examiner

No source labeled lean-left or left covered this story.

Sen. Lee pressures GOP leaders to cancel or delay August recess until election-security bill passes.

Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) is pressuring Republican leaders to cancel or delay the upcoming August recess until the SAVE America Act is passed. The measure would require voters to prove their U.S. citizenship and provide a valid photo ID when registering, and it would restrict voting by mail. Lee has posted on X, requesting that Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) cancel or delay the recess and calling for a roll call vote.

Thune has indicated that he may consider delaying or canceling the recess if there is a likelihood of passing the SAVE Act. However, he also stated that if there's no clear path for passage, there's no reason to keep lawmakers in Washington. Thune noted that vulnerable GOP incumbents need to get back to their home states to campaign ahead of the November election.

Several other Senate Republicans have expressed support for canceling the recess and focusing on passing the SAVE America Act. Sens. Rick Scott (R-Fla.), Ashley Moody (R-Fla.), and Jim Banks (R-Ind.) have all announced their intent to object to Thune calling for recess until the bill is passed.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts conflict over the number of senators who support canceling the August recess. Just The News reports that at least six other Senate Republicans support Lee's call, while Washington Examiner states that "several Republican senators and leading proponents of the bill are vowing to oppose a vote to leave for recess." New York Post also mentions that several Republican senators have expressed support for canceling the recess.

The accounts also differ in their characterization of Thune's position. Just The News reports that Thune told reporters he wouldn't rule out delaying or canceling the recess, while Washington Examiner states that Thune "warned against wasting time on a bill that has already failed multiple times on the Senate floor." New York Post quotes Thune as saying he wants to prioritize avoiding a government shutdown.

Sources Just The News · Washington Examiner · New York Post

No source labeled left covered this story.

Wildfires rage across southwestern France and Spain as heatwaves return.

Wildfires have been burning out of control in southwestern France and Spain for days, forcing mass evacuations and destroying homes. The blazes have been fueled by hot, dry weather conditions, with temperatures soaring above 40°C (104°F) in some areas. In France, the Gironde fire has burned over 100,000 hectares of land, about four times the size of Paris, and destroyed more than 240 homes. Spanish authorities have declared a national emergency as crews fight fires on two fronts - one west of Madrid and another near Valencia.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts from different outlets conflict in several areas. The Guardian reports that UN climate chief Simon Stiell warned that "the climate alarm is blaring, from every direction" and that the costs of the climate crisis are reaching national emergency levels (Guardian). However, NPR does not mention this warning and instead focuses on the immediate response to the wildfires, including evacuations and firefighting efforts. Al Jazeera reports that over 150,000 hectares have burned across Spain since January, while Straight Arrow News states that authorities evacuated 79,000 people in Spain.

Sources The Guardian · NPR · Al Jazeera · BBC · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

Democratic Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed defends disparaging John Fetterman with ‘ogre on a pike’ comment

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, defended his comments about putting an "ogre" on a pike during a Zoom meeting with donors. The remarks were made in reference to Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), whom El-Sayed accused of getting elected on one set of values and then throwing those values in the mud. El-Sayed claimed that he was not referring to Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), his primary opponent, but rather to Fetterman.

During the debate, moderator Roop Raj asked El-Sayed if he regretted any of the comments he made during the Zoom meeting. El-Sayed declined to apologize and instead argued that he has consistently urged civility among his supporters. He also claimed that he had previously pushed back against unkind treatment of Stevens.

Stevens responded by pointing out that El-Sayed's remarks were not just about Fetterman, but also about his own ambitions for national politics. She accused El-Sayed of being more focused on building a national platform than representing Michigan.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts from New York Post and FOX News report that El-Sayed made the "ogre" comment during a Zoom meeting with donors, while The Daily Wire reports that the audio was obtained by Politico. Washington Examiner and CBS News do not mention the source of the audio. Straight Arrow News does not mention the audio at all.

The accounts from New York Post and FOX News report that El-Sayed's comments were about Fetterman, while The Daily Wire reports that El-Sayed clarified that he meant to refer to Fetterman rather than Stevens. Washington Examiner and CBS News do not mention this clarification.

Sources New York Post · FOX News · The Daily Wire · Washington Examiner · CBS News · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled left covered this story.

ICE to target Haitians as Temporary Protected Status is set to end, sources say.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has made plans to ramp up operations to arrest and deport Haitian migrants, as hundreds of thousands of Haitians brace for the termination of their legal status, according to two agency sources and federal documents obtained by CBS News. The plans include arresting migrants in Ohio — where large Haitian communities in cities like Springfield have been targeted by President Trump and conservative politicians and commentators — and quickly putting them on deportation flights to crisis-stricken Haiti.

The Supreme Court last month sided with the Trump administration in its efforts to end the TPS programs for Haitians and Syrians. That ruling's binding mandate is set to be issued to lower courts on Monday. Since that ruling, fear and uncertainty have swept throughout Haitian communities across the U.S. Immigrants whose TPS lapses immediately lose their ability to work in the country legally, and become eligible to be arrested and processed for deportation by ICE.

The operations targeting Haitian migrants could start as early as this week, the documents suggest, but more details about the scale of the plans were not immediately clear. The ICE sources who described the preparations requested anonymity to describe internal plans that have not been publicly disclosed and are fluid.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News reports that President Trump amplified baseless claims that Haitians in Springfield were eating cats and dogs during the 2024 presidential campaign, while FOX News does not mention this. The Washington Examiner mentions it but attributes it to "President Donald Trump's past comments". CBS News also states that ICE leadership has been notified of the operational plans, which is not mentioned by other outlets.

Sources CBS News · FOX News · The Daily Wire · Washington Examiner

No source labeled left covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Johnson & Johnson proposes $5.5 billion talc settlement to end marathon legal fight, potentially providing significant financial relief to thousands of cancer victims and their families.

Johnson & Johnson proposes $5.5 billion talc settlement to end marathon legal fight

Johnson & Johnson has agreed to pay $5.5 billion to settle remaining lawsuits claiming its talc products caused ovarian cancer. The company, which has been fighting talc-related lawsuits for over a decade, said the settlement is conditioned on at least 95% of remaining claimants participating. A U.S. bankruptcy court judge previously denied a $9 billion settlement proposed by Johnson & Johnson subsidiary Red River Talc last year.

The proposed settlement comes after a federal judge ordered plaintiffs to show why their claims should not be dismissed for failing to provide direct evidence linking the company's product to cancer. Johnson & Johnson has long denied that its talc products caused cancer, saying they were safe and did not contain asbestos. The company stopped selling talc-based baby powder in the US in 2020.

Johnson & Johnson expects to pay $3 billion next year as part of the settlement, with no additional payments due until 2028. The company's vice president of litigation, Erik Haas, said the resolution allows the company to put the matter behind it and remain focused on its mission to develop medicines and devices that save lives.

Where the accounts differ

Associated Press reports that Johnson & Johnson previously settled about 95% of filed lawsuits for mesothelioma, a cancer in the tissue surrounding organs like the lungs and heart. The Guardian does not mention this settlement. UPI mentions that Johnson & Johnson paid $2.5 billion to women whose claims were consolidated in Missouri in 2021, but Associated Press and The Guardian do not report this.

Sources Associated Press · The Guardian · UPI

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

item.content:encoded:
Republicans and Democrats clash for control across the country as midterms approach.

The 2026 midterm elections are just 100 days away, with both parties vying for control of Congress and statehouses. Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in both chambers, but Democrats need a net gain of just six House seats to reclaim the speaker's gavel and four Senate seats to win back the upper chamber.

In the House, Republicans will be bolstered by redistricting wins in states like Florida and Texas, while Democrats are focusing on the economy and affordability in their messaging. A recent Fox News poll showed that 53% of voters would back the Democratic candidate in their House district, a 7-point edge outside the margin of error.

In the Senate, Republicans are looking to hold on to seats in Alaska, North Carolina, Ohio, and Maine, with record amounts of spending already pouring into those states. Democrats hope to capitalize on the historic, economic, foreign policy, and anti-incumbent mood among voters.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts from Fox News and The Guardian differ on the role of Donald Trump in the midterms. Fox News reports that Republicans are looking to tie Democrats to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) in their midterm strategy, while The Guardian suggests that Trump's efforts to undermine the election process could have a significant impact on the outcome.

The accounts from Al Jazeera and BBC differ on the details of the Berlin Pride ramming attack. Al Jazeera reports that one person was killed and 17 injured, while BBC reports that one woman was killed and at least 29 others were injured.

Sources FOX News · The Guardian · Al Jazeera · NPR · BBC · Washington Examiner

US pauses strikes on Iran for third night as Trump weighs diplomatic options

The United States has paused its strikes on Iran for the third consecutive night, with President Donald Trump weighing his next move in the nearly five-month-old conflict. The pause follows a series of attacks and counterattacks between the two countries, which have resulted in dozens of deaths and significant damage to infrastructure.

According to reports, top military officials advised Trump to halt the bombing campaign due to dwindling munitions stockpiles that could hamper a sustained military campaign in the region. Diplomatic negotiations are ongoing to avoid a return to all-out war.

The Iranian army spokesperson announced on Sunday that Tehran had halted "retaliatory" attacks against US allies in the region, citing a pause in US strikes as the reason for this decision.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News reports that President Trump said the U.S. has plenty of ammunition, following concerns about depleted stockpiles. However, The New York Post and Mother Jones report that administration officials have warned about dwindling munitions stockpiles that could hamper a sustained military campaign in the region.

The Christian Science Monitor and BBC report that Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed talks with Oman to manage the safe passage of ships on the Strait of Hormuz. However, The Guardian reports that Iranian officials have demanded payment and control over which ships pass through the strait.

Sources CBS News · Christian Science Monitor · Mother Jones · New York Post · BBC · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Three people killed and one suspect at large in Bite of Seattle food festival shooting

A shooting occurred on Sunday evening during the Bite of Seattle food festival at an events complex near the Space Needle in Seattle, Washington. According to authorities, three people were killed and four others, including a toddler, were wounded. One suspect was arrested, but another remains at large. Investigators believe the two suspects were shooting at each other.

The incident occurred around 6pm local time, when police and ambulances began responding to the scene. Two people died at the scene, and a third person died later at a hospital. The victims included two men, ages 19 and 44, and a 56-year-old woman. Four others were hospitalized, including a 2-year-old boy who was in stable condition.

Where the accounts differ

  • The accounts from various outlets differ in some details:
  • The Guardian reports that the shooting occurred at around 6pm local time, while FOX News reports it happened "shortly after 6 p.m."
  • Just The News and Al Jazeera report that one suspect surrendered at the scene, but FOX News does not mention this detail.
  • The Daily Wire reports that Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson lectured about "gun violence" during a press conference, but other outlets do not mention this.
  • The accounts from various outlets also differ in their descriptions of the victims and the injuries sustained.

Sources The Guardian · BBC · Just The News · The Daily Wire · Al Jazeera · FOX News

Mitch McConnell's prolonged absence stalls Senate legislation.

Mitch McConnell's extended absence from Washington, D.C., has stalled several legislative packages in the Senate. The party holds only a 53-to-47 majority in the Senate, making every vote critical. McConnell's absence, since a fall and subsequent hospitalization on June 14, has raised scrutiny from GOP colleagues worried about advancing bills before the deadline for the usual appropriations process on Oct. 1. If Congress does not pass the annual appropriations bill by Sept. 30, a partial government shutdown will ensue.

McConnell chairs the Senate Appropriations Defense Subcommittee, making his voice a critical one on the panel, which has fallen into partisan deadlock due to his absence. The Appropriations Committee is split 14-14 between Democrats and Republicans, making it essentially impossible to advance controversial legislation. Senate Democrats have made it a negotiating tactic to not support advancing appropriations bills unless increases for the military are paired with similar increases for domestic programs.

The Agriculture Committee's work to advance the "farm bill," an omnibus, multiyear law that governs an array of agricultural and food programs, has also stalled, as McConnell is the second-ranking Republican on the panel. Republicans don't have enough votes without McConnell to advance it out of the Senate Agriculture Committee, since his absence leaves the panel at 11-11.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts conflict over the extent of McConnell's absence and its impact on legislation. The Washington Examiner reports that McConnell's absence has stalled high-stakes legislative packages, while FOX News notes that McConnell is still recovering from a medical emergency but has not provided a hard date for his return to Congress.

The New York Post quotes President Trump urging Senate Majority Leader John Thune to keep the chamber in session until it passes the SAVE America Act or ends the filibuster. However, The Hill reports that Thune has repeatedly pushed back on this demand by declaring there aren't nearly enough Republican votes to abolish the filibuster rule.

Newsweek provides a health update from Senator McConnell's doctor, stating that he is undergoing multiple physical therapy and rehabilitation sessions each day aimed at rebuilding strength and reducing the risk of future falls. However, the Washington Examiner reports that McConnell's absence has complicated sensitive negotiations to bring back an expired provision of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA).

Sources Washington Examiner · FOX News · New York Post · The Hill · Newsweek

No source labeled lean-left or left covered this story.

Wildfires force over 300,000 people to evacuate homes in France and Spain.

Wildfires are raging across southwestern Europe, forcing more than 300,000 people to flee their homes. The blazes have burned vast areas of land in France and Spain, with authorities deploying thousands of firefighters to battle the fires. In France, over 220,000 people have been evacuated from their homes, while in Spain, around 75,000 people have been forced to leave.

The wildfires are among the worst in France since World War II, with some areas experiencing unprecedented heatwaves and droughts. The blazes have also affected the Tour de France, with the final stage of the cycling race being shortened due to the fires. In Spain, a fast-moving wildfire killed at least 12 people on July 10.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts from different outlets conflict in several areas. NPR reports that over 250,000 people have been evacuated in France and Spain, while Al Jazeera states that more than 325,000 people have been forced to flee their homes. The Hill reports that no deaths have been tied to the fires, but CBS News mentions a person killed in the town of Manises in Spain.

NPR also provides specific numbers for the area burned by wildfires in France and Spain, stating that over 242,000 acres have been ravaged in France this year, while Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said that more than 300,000 acres have already burned in Spain. The Guardian reports that at least 240 homes in Gironde have been totally destroyed by the wildfire.

Sources NPR · BBC · The Hill · CBS News · The Guardian · Al Jazeera

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Federal appeals court rejects Trump bid to enforce mail ballot order ahead of midterm elections.

A federal appeals court on Saturday refused to let the Trump administration enforce key parts of President Donald Trump's executive order tightening mail-in voting rules in 23 Democratic-led states. The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals denied the Department of Justice's request to pause a June ruling blocking several provisions of Trump's March executive order while the administration appeals. The court found that the plaintiff states were already facing looming election deadlines and had begun preparing for potential changes.

The lawsuit was brought by 23 states and the District of Columbia, led by California, Massachusetts, Nevada, and Washington. They argue that the Constitution gives them primary responsibility for administering federal elections and that the president exceeded his authority by directing federal agencies to impose new voting requirements. U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani agreed in June, ruling that several provisions of the executive order likely exceeded the president's authority and blocking federal agencies from implementing them in the plaintiff states through the Nov. 3 federal elections.

The Trump administration argued that the lawsuit was premature because federal agencies had not finalized the policies needed to implement the executive order. However, the appeals court rejected this argument, stating that the plaintiff states have no practical choice but to respond to the order now due to rapidly approaching deadlines.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News and The Hill report that the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals made a 2-1 decision, while Washington Examiner reports it as a "declined" request to lift an injunction. Just The News does not mention the vote count in its report. FOX News attributes criticism of the ruling to Ohio Congressman Jim Jordan, while The Hill mentions Trump's July primetime address on election integrity.

Sources FOX News · Washington Examiner · New York Post · Just The News · The Guardian · The Hill

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Dr. Anthony Fauci's diary entries reveal fixation on fame during COVID-19 pandemic.

Dr. Anthony Fauci's diary entries, released by Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.), show a growing obsession with his public profile and media appearances as the COVID-19 pandemic raged on. The entries, spanning from December 2019 to December 2022, reveal Fauci's fixation on being in the spotlight, even as the death toll mounted worldwide.

Fauci's diary entries detail his interactions with President Donald Trump, governors, and world leaders, as well as his media appearances and personal observations during the pandemic. A recurring theme throughout the diaries is Fauci's growing awareness of his own public profile, which he described as "explosive and really unimaginable" by May 2020.

As the attention continued to grow, Fauci's diary entries documented how his prominence had expanded beyond public health. He noted that Secret Service agents had become so familiar with him they often waved him through White House security without checking his identification.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts from The Daily Wire and New York Post report that Fauci wrote about being invited to appear on "Dancing with the Stars" in June 2020, while The Hill reports this invitation occurred a month later. The Federalist notes that CNN appears 275 times in Fauci's diary, while other outlets do not mention this specific detail.

The Guardian reports that Fauci described Trump as "rambling", "crazy", and "an idiot" in his diary entries, while other outlets focus on Fauci's fixation on fame. The Hill mentions that Fauci received a letter from Barbra Streisand expressing her appreciation for his guidance during the pandemic, but does not provide further details.

Sources The Daily Wire · New York Post · The Guardian · The Federalist · The Hill · FOX News

No source labeled lean-left or lean-right covered this story.

ICE To Target Haitians As Their Temporary Protected Status Expires

The US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is planning to target Haitian nationals whose Temporary Protected Status (TPS) is set to expire. Over 300,000 Haitians have been living in the US under TPS since 2010 due to turmoil in their home country. The Trump administration has argued that the program was never intended to be a permanent form of legal status.

The Supreme Court recently ruled in favor of the administration's efforts to terminate TPS for Haitians and Syrians, paving the way for ICE to begin enforcing deportations. According to internal documents obtained by CBS News, ICE plans to ramp up operations to arrest and deport Haitian migrants, with a focus on Ohio where large Haitian communities have been targeted by President Trump.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts from The Daily Wire, The Guardian, FOX News, and CBS News all report that the TPS for Haitians is set to expire. However, there are some discrepancies in the numbers of Haitians affected: The Daily Wire reports 300,000, while The Guardian reports over 330,000.

Additionally, The Guardian attributes a characterization of the Trump administration's decision to end TPS as "racist" to Roxana Rivera, assistant to the president at Service Employees International Union (SEIU) 32BJ. This claim is not made by any other outlet.

The Daily Wire and CBS News both report that ICE plans to target Haitian migrants in Ohio, but The Guardian does not mention this specific detail.

Sources The Daily Wire · The Guardian · FOX News · CBS News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Cyclospora cases mounting in Michigan due to Trump admin cuts compromising food safety.

Cyclospora cases mounting in Michigan

Cyclospora cases have been reported in multiple states, including Michigan, where the outbreak is particularly severe. The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) has confirmed at least 7,400 cases of cyclospora, with many originating from Michigan and Ohio. State and local health officials are working to identify the cause of the outbreak, which may be linked to contaminated iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms in central Mexico.

The CDC has reported that cyclospora is generally transmitted through food or water contamination, rather than direct person-to-person contact. The parasite requires days or weeks to become infectious, making it difficult to track and contain outbreaks. In this case, the outbreak is believed to have originated from contaminated iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms.

The FDA has launched an investigation into the outbreak, which has affected nine states so far. Taylor Farms has recalled its products and temporarily suspended production at its central Mexico facility.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News reports that there are over 11,000 cases of cyclospora reported in 41 states, while The Hill mentions a total of 7,400 confirmed cases. CBS News also quotes Susan Mayne as saying that the outbreak is "record-setting," which is not mentioned in The Hill's account.

Sources The Hill · CBS News

No source labeled lean-right or left or right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

item.content:encoded:
At least 1 dead, several injured after van rams into crowd at Pride festival

A white van rammed into a crowd of people attending a Pride festival in Berlin on Saturday evening, killing one person and injuring at least 16 others. The incident occurred during the European city's annual Christopher Street Day festival, an LGBTQ+ Pride event that attracts hundreds of thousands of people. Police said they have identified a suspect who is known to them and has links to "Islamic circles" in Berlin.

The attack happened around 10pm local time at Tiergarten Park, near the iconic Brandenburg Gate. The van crashed into a tree after hitting several people, and police later found the vehicle abandoned at the scene. Emergency services treated the injured, with some suffering life-threatening injuries.

Police launched an intensive manhunt for the suspect, who is believed to be armed and dangerous. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz condemned the incident as "a heinous act" on social media, saying that it was an attack on society's values of kindness and tolerance.

Where the accounts differ

  • The number of injured people reported by different outlets varies: 16 (FOX News), 17 (NPR), 29 (BBC).
  • The BBC reports that the suspect is a 21-year-old German citizen of Lebanese background, while other outlets do not provide this information.
  • The Washington Examiner mentions that police raided an apartment in connection with the investigation, but does not specify whether anyone was found there.

Sources FOX News · The Guardian · Al Jazeera · NPR · BBC · Washington Examiner

Trump delivers jokes and jabs at White House Correspondents' Association Dinner

President Donald Trump attended the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) Dinner on July 24, 2026, at the Waldorf Astoria hotel in Washington D.C. The event was originally scheduled for April but was disrupted by an assassination attempt on the president. Trump's speech included jokes and jabs at the press, politicians, and himself. He praised the Secret Service and law enforcement officers who responded to the April shooting, awarding Officer Victor Gonzales with the WHCA President's Award for Exceptional Service.

Trump also quipped about his relationship with the press, saying "sometimes I really do think that some of you don't like me." He joked that when he leaves office, the news industry will be "broke" because there won't be anyone to report on. Trump produced a "Trump 2028" hat and said he would run for a fourth term as president.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post reports that Trump mocked California Governor Gavin Newsom's 2028 White House ambitions, claiming Newsom had doomed himself with praise for Kamala Harris. The Guardian notes that Trump is reviving old tropes about communism and has identified it as the US's biggest threat.

FOX News highlights Trump's jokes at the press and members of his cabinet, including a quip about Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. cutting up a cow to bring beef tenderloin for dinner. The BBC reports that Trump took swipes at the press during the dinner, but also praised the Secret Service and law enforcement officers who responded to the April shooting.

The Hill notes that Trump's speech included a tribute to the U.S. Secret Service, law enforcement officers, and hotel staff who responded to the April incident. CBS News reports that Trump cracked jokes at reporters and politicians during the event, but also acknowledged the sometimes-tense relationship with the press.

Sources New York Post · FOX News · The Guardian · BBC · The Hill · CBS News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Maine Democrats crown Troy Jackson as Platner replacement as fresh scrutiny clouds Senate reset

Troy Jackson was elected as the Maine Democratic Party's nominee for U.S. Senate on Saturday at a nominating convention in Bangor. He will face Republican incumbent Susan Collins in November. Jackson, a former state Senate president and fifth-generation logger, won 566 of 571 delegate votes to secure the nomination.

The selection comes after Graham Platner dropped out of the race earlier this month due to allegations of sexual assault made by a former girlfriend. Platner denied the accusations but withdrew from the campaign.

Jackson's nomination caps an abbreviated process to find a replacement for Platner, who was backed by progressive champion and Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont. Jackson has been endorsed by Sanders in his past campaigns and supports progressive policies such as Medicare for All and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that there are concerns within the party about Jackson's alleged temper and workplace conduct, while NPR notes that these allegations have not led to significant public pushback from state leaders.

CBS News highlights the abbreviated process to find a replacement for Platner, which was triggered by his withdrawal from the race. The New York Post notes that many viewed Jackson as the favorite to succeed Platner due to his populist brand of politics.

The Daily Wire criticizes the Maine Democratic Party's decision-making process, suggesting that Jackson was hand-selected without a single vote being cast by Mainers.

Sources FOX News · NPR · CBS News · The New York Post · The Daily Wire

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Iran-backed Houthis claim missile attack on Saudi Arabia as regional tensions escalate

The Iranian-backed Houthi rebels claimed a missile attack on the southern Saudi city of Jizan on Saturday, after vowing retaliation against the kingdom for attacks this week. The US and Iran have been engaged in a series of strikes over the past two weeks, with the US carrying out 13 consecutive nights of attacks on Iran. Iranian officials have publicly pushed back against US pressure while divisions persist inside Tehran over whether diplomacy or confrontation is the best path forward.

The Houthis said the attack was retaliation for Saudi airstrikes on Houthi targets in the Yemeni port city of Hodeida and a nearby island on Friday. The group had vowed to target ships attempting to transit the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. The US military has fired on and disabled a tanker ship in the Gulf of Oman that was attempting to evade the American blockade on Iranian ports.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post reports that President Trump halted new US strikes on Iran as he weighs whether Tehran is ready to cut a deal, while the BBC states that there were no overnight reports of air strikes in the wider region by the US or Iran for the first time in two weeks. The Christian Science Monitor notes that the conflict is threatening to disrupt international shipping through the Red Sea.

Sources The Guardian · The Hill · New York Post · BBC · Christian Science Monitor · Just The News

More than 300,000 flee homes due to wildfires in France and Spain.

Wildfires have forced over 300,000 people to evacuate their homes in France and Spain. The fires have been burning for days, fueled by strong winds and high temperatures. In France, more than 167,000 people had been evacuated as of Saturday night, with the most devastating fires in the Southwest, particularly in the Gironde and Landes regions. French President Emmanuel Macron said that the situation remains critical in the Gironde department.

In Spain, at least one person has died from the fires, and over 60,000 people were evacuated from Avila and near Madrid. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez declared a national state of emergency due to the wildfires. The final stage of the Tour de France was shortened due to the fires, with security forces redeployed to assist with the response.

Where the accounts differ

  • NPR reports that over 242,000 acres have been burned in France this year, a historic record, according to French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. The Guardian does not mention this specific figure.
  • The BBC quotes EU Commissioner for Crisis Management Hadja Lahbib as saying that last year one million hectares burned during the summer and they are expecting another historical record. This is also reported by NPR but not by other outlets.
  • CBS News reports that at least 197,000 people have been evacuated in France due to the wildfires, which French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said was "probably" the biggest peacetime evacuation the country has seen. The Guardian and BBC do not mention this specific figure.

Sources NPR · The Guardian · BBC · The Hill · CBS News · Al Jazeera

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

India's Education Minister Resigns Amid Nationwide Protests Over Exam Leaks and Education Reforms

India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned on Saturday after weeks of protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth movement that has been demanding education reforms, compensation for families of students who died by suicide due to exam leaks, and accountability from the government. The protests began in May after allegations of leaks in some of India's biggest entrance exams.

The CJP, which started as a satirical campaign on social media, has grown into a powerful platform for young people's anxieties and dissent. Its founder, Abhijeet Dipke, rallied tens of thousands of students and supporters in New Delhi to force Pradhan's resignation. The movement has been marked by widespread protests, sit-ins, and hunger strikes across the country.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts from different outlets highlight some differences in emphasis and reporting. NPR focuses on the government's shift in tactics and the role of Milan Vaishnav, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, who suggests that the government realized its usual playbook was not working. The Guardian emphasizes the significance of Pradhan's resignation as a major victory for the CJP and a challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's strongman image.

Sources NPR · The Guardian · BBC · Al Jazeera · Washington Examiner · CBS News

No source labeled right covered this story.

Federal appeals court rejects Trump bid to enforce key parts of mail-in voting order ahead of midterm elections.

A federal appeals court on Saturday refused to let the Trump administration enforce key parts of President Donald Trump's executive order tightening mail-in voting rules in 23 Democratic-led states. The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to lift a lower-court injunction from June that ruled parts of the president's order was unconstitutional after Democratic-led states, including California, Massachusetts and Washington, sued the administration.

The appeals court rejected the administration's appeal in a 2-1 decision. The Trump order directed the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to compile lists of confirmed U.S. citizens eligible to vote and provide them to states, instructs the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) to establish new standards for mail-in ballots and directs the Justice Department to prioritize investigations into state and local election officials who issue federal ballots to people deemed ineligible to vote.

The lawsuit was brought by 23 states and the District of Columbia, led by California, Massachusetts, Nevada and Washington. The states argue the Constitution gives them primary responsibility for administering federal elections and that the president exceeded his authority by directing federal agencies to impose new voting requirements.

Where the accounts differ

  • FOX News and New York Post both report on Congressman Jim Jordan's criticism of the ruling, but only FOX News provides a quote from him.
  • The Hill reports on President Trump's July primetime address on election integrity, while The Guardian mentions his claims about widespread voter fraud in 2020.

Sources FOX News · Washington Examiner · New York Post · The Hill · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Israeli forces detain over 70 people in West Bank after deadly clashes between soldiers and Palestinian villagers.

At least four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers were killed in a shootout in the northern village of Tal in the occupied West Bank. The incident occurred when a group of about 20 Israeli settlers, many armed, approached the village with the intent to cause violence. Villagers confronted the settlers, and as tensions rose, Israeli soldiers arrived on the scene. A Palestinian man grabbed a gun from one of the settlers, leading to a shootout that resulted in the deaths of four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers.

The Israeli military confirmed that it had arrested more than 70 people across the West Bank overnight and into Saturday, with troops remaining in the village of Tell where the clashes erupted. The arrests were part of a wider crackdown on Palestinian residents, with reports of widespread searches and raids at hospitals and homes.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts from different outlets diverge in their descriptions of the events leading up to the shootout. The BBC reports that Palestinians confronted Jewish settlers who were attacking them, while Israel's military said it had responded to reports that hikers had been attacked. Al Jazeera states that a group of about 20 Israeli settlers approached the village with the intent to cause violence.

Sources The Hill · BBC · Al Jazeera

No source labeled left or right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: An 83-year-old man who went missing near the Grand Canyon was rescued after an overnight search.

Man, 83, who went missing near Grand Canyon rescued after overnight search

Gerald Guinn, an 83-year-old man from Utah, was hiking with another person in a remote location on the edge of the Kaibab National Forest at the Grand Canyon National Park. They split up to search for a nearby historic object, but Guinn never reunited with his companion. The other hiker searched for several hours before requesting help.

The Kane County Sheriff's Office Search and Rescue team conducted an overnight search using drones and search dogs, but found no sign of Guinn. The next morning, the Grand Canyon National Park Service took over the search efforts, adding a helicopter and ground teams to the search. A cell phone ping indicated Guinn's general location, leading the NPS to move the search to the east.

The NPS helicopter located Guinn, who was well enough to wave to the pilot. However, due to the terrain, the helicopter could not land, so a Kane County search and rescue team was sent to assess and stabilize Guinn.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News reports that the operation was completed at 1:30 a.m., about a day and a half after Guinn first began his hike. FOX News does not provide this specific time frame.

Sources CBS News · FOX News

No source labeled center or lean-right or left covered this story.

The brief ends here.

Secret Service Increases Security for Rescheduled White House Correspondents' Association Dinner

The rescheduled White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) dinner took place on July 24, 2026, at the Waldorf Astoria hotel in Washington D.C. The event was originally scheduled for April 25 but was postponed after an armed assailant attempted to assassinate President Donald Trump and other officials during the first dinner. Secret Service Director Sean Curran stated that the agency has seen a surge in threats against its protectees, with approximately 10,000 protective intelligence cases opened since January.

The rescheduled event featured enhanced security measures, including airport-style magnetometer screening for all ticketed guests, a visible police presence around the hotel, and traffic closures due to proximity to major thoroughfares. The Secret Service also implemented a separate entrance for guests rather than using the main lobby.

During the dinner, President Trump delivered a speech that included jokes at the expense of the press and his political opponents. He praised the Secret Service and law enforcement officers who responded to the April shooting, awarding Officer Victor Gonzales with the WHCA President's Award for Exceptional Service.

Where the accounts differ

  • The Daily Wire reports that the event was streamed live on their platform, while other outlets do not mention this detail.
  • New York Post focuses primarily on Trump's jokes and criticisms of his opponents, whereas other accounts provide more balanced coverage of the event.
  • FOX News highlights the heartfelt moments between Trump and the press, including a speech by ABC's Jon Karl praising the president for attending the dinner. This is not mentioned in other outlets.
  • BBC notes that the event was considerably scaled down from the first correspondents' dinner, with about 700 people in attendance compared to over 2,000 in April.

Sources The Daily Wire · New York Post · FOX News · BBC · The Hill · CBS News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Iran-backed Houthis claim missile attack on Saudi Arabia as regional tensions escalate

The Iranian-backed Houthi rebels claimed a missile attack on the southern Saudi city of Jizan on Saturday, after vowing retaliation against the kingdom for attacks this week. The US military did not announce fresh strikes on Iran on Saturday, having carried out 13 consecutive nights of attacks on the country. During this time, Iran has also launched drone strikes on US military facilities and bases across the Middle East.

The Houthis said the attack was a "dangerous escalation" in response to Saudi airstrikes on Houthi targets in Yemen. The group had vowed retaliation after Riyadh launched air strikes on Hodeida and Kamaran island on Friday. The Saudi civil defence also issued warnings for the port city of Jizan, close to the border with Yemen.

The US has imposed a new round of tariffs on 59 countries and the European Union, citing imports made with forced labor. The ongoing conflict between the US and Iran has led to increased tensions in the region, with oil prices surging to $100 per barrel after the Houthis attacked two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea.

Where the accounts differ

  • The New York Post reports that President Trump halted new US strikes on Iran as he weighs whether Tehran is ready to cut a deal, while the BBC states that there were no overnight reports of air strikes in the wider region by the US or Iran for the first time in two weeks.
  • The Christian Science Monitor notes that the Houthis' naval blockade against Saudi Arabia has raised concerns about global oil supplies, while the NPR article focuses on the impact of the conflict on everyday people and the economy.
  • The Hill reports that the escalating war with Iran is threatening to depress Republican turnout ahead of the midterms, while the other outlets focus on the military and economic aspects of the conflict.

Sources The Guardian · BBC · New York Post · Christian Science Monitor · NPR

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

At least 1 dead, several injured after van rams into crowd at Pride festival in Berlin.

A white van rammed into a crowd at the Christopher Street Day festival in Berlin on Saturday evening, killing one person and injuring at least 16 others. The incident occurred during the annual LGBTQ+ Pride event, which was attended by hundreds of thousands of people. Police were quick to respond, canceling the event and urging everyone to leave the area.

According to police, a suspect has been identified as a member of Berlin's "Islamist scene," but they have not yet been arrested. The motive behind the attack is still unknown. Emergency services treated the injured at the scene, with some victims having life-threatening injuries.

Berlin Mayor Kai Wegner described the incident as an "attack on our free and cosmopolitan society." German Chancellor Friedrich Merz vowed to punish those responsible, saying he and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt would "push to make sure this horrific act is fully investigated and punished."

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that police had detained someone involved with the "Islamist scene in Berlin," but it's unclear if they were the driver of the van. The Guardian mentions a witness who said a man emerged from the vehicle and fled on foot, but this detail is not present in other accounts.

Sources FOX News · The Guardian · Al Jazeera · NPR · CBS News · Washington Examiner

Maine Democrats formally nominate Troy Jackson as their new candidate for U.S. Senate.

Troy Jackson was formally nominated by the Maine Democratic Party to run against Republican Senator Susan Collins in the upcoming election. Jackson, a former state Senate President and fifth-generation logger, won the nomination with 566 votes out of 571 delegates at the party's convention in Bangor. He replaces Graham Platner, who dropped out of the race after allegations of sexual assault surfaced.

Jackson has been endorsed by progressive champion Bernie Sanders and has run on an economic populist message, emphasizing issues like Medicare for All and raising taxes on the ultra-wealthy. However, his nomination has also raised concerns about his past behavior, including reports of a short temper and alleged mortgage improprieties.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News notes that some Democrats have expressed concern about Jackson's vetting process, with one strategist saying "it's very clear that Democrats should not be looking to Maine to flip the Senate." In contrast, NPR quotes Democratic state Sen. Stacy Brenner as saying that Jackson has evolved on issues like reproductive rights and is a strong candidate.

The Guardian notes that Jackson's nomination caps a chaotic search for a replacement after Platner's withdrawal, and highlights his unusual political biography as a champion of rural workers. CBS News emphasizes the abbreviated timeline for finding a new nominee, with only two weeks to select a candidate before the July 27 deadline.

New York Post reports on the swift coronation of Jackson, noting that he was essentially guaranteed the nomination after most delegates pledged their support. The Daily Wire criticizes the process as undemocratic, pointing out that not a single Mainer voted for Jackson as the nominee.

Sources FOX News · NPR · The Guardian · CBS News · New York Post · The Daily Wire

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

US imposes new tariffs on 60 trading partners as temporary duties expire

The US has imposed new tariffs on 60 trading partners, including the UK, China, and the European Union, in a move that replaces a temporary global tariff that expired on Friday. The new levies range from 10% to 12.5% and are intended to be more legally durable than their predecessors. The tariffs are based on claims that key economic partners have failed to properly tackle forced labor.

The new duties apply to the top 60 US trade partners, covering 99.4% of US imports, according to the Office of the US Trade Representative. Trading partners that have taken steps to ban forced labor face tariffs of 10%, while those countries that do not effectively prohibit the practice have a rate of 12.5%.

The move has been met with criticism from some quarters, with experts warning that it could lead to higher costs for businesses and consumers.

Where the accounts differ

  • The Hill emphasizes the potential political impact of the tariffs on Republican candidates in the midterms, while other outlets focus more on the economic implications.
  • NPR notes that the new tariffs are not significantly higher than their predecessors, but still higher than when Trump's second term started.
  • Fox Business highlights the fact that many products will be exempt from the tariffs, including oil and gas, fertilizer, and certain food products.

Sources BBC · The Hill · NPR · CBS News · Fox Business

No source labeled right covered this story.

Trump orders signs outside Smithsonian warning of "inaccurate" information about American history.

President Donald Trump has ordered the installation of signs outside the National Museum of American History at the Smithsonian Institution, warning visitors that the exhibits may contain "inaccurate" information. The order is part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to push back against what it sees as a politicized and biased approach to American history.

The move comes after a report released by the White House's Domestic Policy Council accused the museum's leadership of adopting an ideological framework that prioritizes social justice over historical accuracy. The report, titled "Saving America's Story," claims that the museum views American history as a "prime tool" for advancing ideas of social justice and transforming society.

The Smithsonian Institution has defended its approach to American history, with Director Anthea Hartig stating that the museum aims to tell the truth about the country's past, including its failures to live up to its founding ideals. However, the Trump administration sees this approach as a threat to traditional values and is pushing for a more patriotic and celebratory narrative of American history.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts from FOX News and The Guardian differ in their characterization of the Smithsonian's approach to American history. FOX News portrays the museum's leadership as promoting a "woke" ideology that seeks to divide Americans, while The Guardian describes the institution's efforts to tell a more nuanced and accurate story about the country's past.

Sources FOX News · The Guardian · BBC · CBS News · The Daily Wire

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

More than 250,000 people flee wildfires in France and Spain.

Devastating wildfires in Spain and France have forced more than 250,000 people to evacuate. In France, over 197,000 people were evacuated, with the interior minister describing it as "probably" the biggest peacetime evacuation the country has seen. The fires have also affected the Tour de France, with the route for the final stage shortened due to security and police being reassigned to assist with the fires.

In Spain, a national state of emergency was declared, and at least one person died in a fire in Manises, Valencia. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said that his government is working to provide shelter for those who evacuated or were confined because of the fires. The fires have burned down over 130,000 hectares of forest this year in Spain, which is about a third higher than the country's annual average.

Where the accounts differ

NPR reports that more than 167,000 people had been evacuated from France as of Saturday night, while The Guardian states that 197,000 people fled in France. BBC reports that over 300,000 people have fled fires in France and Spain, which is higher than the numbers reported by NPR and The Guardian.

India's education minister resigns after student protests over exam leaks and testing irregularities.

India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned on Saturday, meeting one of the key demands of students who have been protesting for weeks over allegations of failing to prevent leaks of medical school entrance exams. The protests, led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth movement that challenges Prime Minister Narendra Modi's handling of youth unemployment and educational opportunities, began in May after it was alleged that entrance exams had been leaked and sold to certain students.

The CJP called for an end to the weekslong effort to oust Pradhan after his announcement. The protests stemmed from allegations that entrance exams to highly competitive medical schools had been leaked and sold to certain students, forcing millions to retake the tests. Abhijeet Dipke, a Boston University graduate and the party's founder, rallied tens of thousands of students and supporters in New Delhi beginning in May to force Pradhan's resignation and demand compensation for the families of students who committed suicide after being affected by the entrance exam scandal.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts from NPR and The Guardian emphasize the significance of the protests as a challenge to Modi's government, while the BBC and Al Jazeera focus on the specific demands of the protesters. Washington Examiner highlights the economic implications of the protests for young people in India.
